name: Near black
lede: Near black is a black with a trace of color in it, which is how some painters, from Gauguin on, made their darkest darks.

sections.title: Mixed blacks
sections.body:
The word has a history in painting. Pastoureau notes that from Gauguin onward some painters gave up the standard blacks (carbon, lamp, bone and ivory black, even the new aniline black) [1]. Instead they combined blue, red and green pigments, such as ultramarine, Prussian blue, cochineal, madder lake, emerald green and malachite, to get near-blacks with many shades in them [1]. See [[prussian-blue]] and [[irresistible]] for two of those ingredients, and [[black]] and [[jet]] for the flat extremes.

As a swatch, #070D0D is a name from the xkcd color survey of 2010 [2]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 would call the position "brownish black" (block 65), 3.8 CIEDE2000 units away [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Near black is the most common dark in the archive. A color near it appears in 3,604 of our 23,781 paintings, 15.15%, more often than 99% of the named colors, as photographed [3]. In 77% of the 3,192 paintings where the within-painting lens finds it, it plays a shadow [3]. Among the painters, 24 of Rembrandt's 50 works here carry it, and 6 of Robert Henri's 12 [3]. In printed English the phrase peaks in the 1900s [4]. Aged varnish darkens shadows, so read these as screen colors [3].
